extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, clergy/divines, and natural philosophers engaged in apologetic debates with atheists
extracted.subtask_description: A series of theological-philosophical arguments defending the possibility of resurrection and the inference of God's wisdom from natural phenomena, addressing objections drawn from natural philosophy and ignorance. Targets readers debating atheism or reconciling scripture with contemporary natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible body is not necessarily the 'own' body
rubrics_metrics.description: A visible Body, though never so much emaciated, can yet be in no Sense esteemed an own Body, as long as there are any Fluids therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a criterion in discussions of identity at resurrection: the presence or absence of humours/juices distinguishes an 'own' body from a mere visible corpse. Example reasoning contrasts emaciated bodies and those divested of juices; see Sect. XXII and XXIII references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nourishment comes from fluids/juices, not solid particles
rubrics_metrics.description: What we make use of for Food does belong only to the vile Body of an Animal, and the Fluids that are therein... the solid Particles belonging to those Bodies upon which we feed, are separated from the Nutritious Juices, and pass off through the Body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical examples: gravy and soup yield nourishment whereas solid particles are separated and pass off. Applied to the cannibal objection: only juices are assimilated, so solids of devoured bodies may remain separable for resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resurrection identity preserved despite prior consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Since all that serves for the Food and Nourishment of a Man-eater must only be divided from the visible Body of the Person devoured... the solid Particles divested of all their Juices, or the own Bodies of the devoured Person, would be discharged, or cast out unmingled with those of the Devourers and consequently that each of them might appear separate and entire at the Time of its Resurrection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument addresses supposed paradoxes (e.g., cannibalism): physiological separation during digestion (juices assimilated, solids evacuated) plausibly leaves the devoured body's 'own' particles unmingled for reappearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert disagreement signals genuine unknowns
rubrics_metrics.description: The different Opinions which prevail among the greatest and most learned Men, about the Causes of the same Appearances, prove this Assertion plain enough: there are an unexpressible Number of Things in the Visible World, as yet unknown to all Men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disagreement among leading mathematicians, astronomers, and natural philosophers (cited examples: differing explanations, confessions of ignorance by eminent figures) as evidence that many natural phenomena remain unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workmanship in a single instance suffices to infer a Maker's skill
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wisdom and Skill of an Artificer is not so much displayed by the Number of Things he has made, as by the Contrivance and Workmanship that appears in each of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: one well-made watch or one complete picture suffices to infer the maker's skill. Applied to theology: a few clear instances of contrivance in nature suffice to infer divine wisdom despite many unknowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unknown things do not refute design (atheistic evasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among these unhappy Men there are some, who to elude the Proofs of a Wise God... endeavour to screen themselves against the Reproaches of their convinced Minds behind these unknown Things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal: pointing out that invoking unknowns is a rhetorical tactic; known instances of order/contrivance remain sufficient to establish design. Two key replies are (1) workmanship suffices, (2) ignorance of structure does not negate evident contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural and poetic appeals to unknowns legitimately magnify divine wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wisdom of his Holy Word... makes use of Things that are unknown to Men, and even inscrutable, in order to convince us of the infinite Perfections of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Psalm 139 and Job's rebukes are cited alongside natural-philosophical observations (embryology from Harvey, Malpighi) to show congruence between scripture's appeal to the wondrous/unknown and modern discoveries; used to strengthen apologetic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to trace material genealogy implies epistemic humility
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither he, nor any one else can ever be able to trace this his Genealogy or Pedigree; nor to say in what Figure, in what Structure, or in what Places the Parts of his present Body have resided from the Beginning of the World.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracing constituent particles back through food, plants, animals, earth, water, and air leads to complex histories beyond human knowledge; thus claims of comprehensive understanding are unwarranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical hypotheses are often pragmatic models, not guarantees of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that the Hypotheses should be even probable, and that it is enough if the Calculations may thereby be made to agree with the Experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copernicus' preface and other authorities are cited to show that astronomers may adopt hypotheses that aid calculation; usefulness or computational convenience should not be conflated with ontological truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of consensus among astronomers about Earth's motion undermines certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Since these great Men... do still differ so much among themselves about the same, can any one believe that they would not long since have agreed in one and the same Opinion, if it had been fully and rightly proved?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples invoked: Philolaus vs Ptolemy, Tycho vs Kepler, remarks about Copernicus, and varied modern positions show persistent disagreement; used as an argument against claiming certainty about Earth's motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of uncertainty by authorities is stronger evidence than mere disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The most famous and most skilful Astronomers, after having employed so much Pains in this Inquiry, do freely and honestly confess, that they are still entirely uncertain, concerning the Motion or Rest of the Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations from Huygens, Newton, Herigonus, de la Hire, Varignon, etc., are used to show that leading practitioners explicitly refrain from asserting certainty; this humility is taken as evidence that no conclusive proof exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model choice principle: prefer hypothesis that simplifies explanation or calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: An Astronomer may choose that which is most easily comprehended... It is more convenient to allow the Sun to be in the Center of the World, because other Phenomena may be more easily and rationally solv'd thereby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors (Stevin, Kepler) acknowledge choosing hypotheses for convenience; warns readers not to conflate convenience with truth, and to be cautious in inferring ontological claims from pragmatic choices.
